speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: FARMERS-STATEMENT ON NET WORTH PORTION OF RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago I promised to make a statement with reference to farmers' income tax returns, and I am now ready to implement that promise. Further consideration has been given to the matter concerning the net worth statement set out in the 1947 T.l prairie farmers and farmers' income tax returns.
I cannot emphasize too strongly that it is in the farmer's own interest as a citizen and taxpayer to provide accurate and complete information of his activities so that he can be dealt with in the same way as every other taxpayer in the country.

The department has placed in the hands of the farmer guide books which should prove of great value in maintaining proper information as to the operation of his farming business, and therefore should be of great help to him in completing his tax return. It will be beneficial to the farmer if he will carefully read the book and the form and attempt to complete it in its entirety.
It has been. the experience of the department that many farmers reporting income do not maintain book-keeping records of their affairs. Our assessors have found in innumerable instances that, to determine the taxable income of the average farmer, it has been necessary to prepare, with the farmer's assistance, of course, a statement of the farmer's net worth and therefrom to calculate or estimate the taxable income.
To assist the farmer and to facilitate the assessing, the 1947 form was evolved, and included with it on page 5 is a statement of net worth. It was proposed that the farmer would complete this statement at the time he completed the return and that the department's assessors would then be in a position to proceed to the determination of the taxable income expeditiously and, in a great many oases, without further reference to the farmer.
It is now represented that this statement of net worth is too complex and that the average farmer will find it impossible to complete it without assistance. It would be impossible, except at a great cost, to build up the staff of the department to enable officials to call on every farmer in Canada for the purpose of assisting in the preparation of income tax returns.
The department therefore has decided that
(a)	those farmers who report their income for 1947 on a cash basis need not complete the farmer's net worth statement section of the return. There may be individual cases where, after the filing of the return, the department will require from a farmer, as from any other taxpayer, in order to make a proper assessment of his income, a statement of assets and liabilities of his business, or other additional information which, in such cases, will be requested in the usual manner.
(b)	Those farmers who report 1947 incomes on an accrual basis must attach to the return a statement of assets and liabilities, as heretofore, or complete the appropriate parts of the net worth statement attached to the return.
Objections have been raised with reference to net worth statement for fishermen. The adjustment of this matter is being given consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated earlier in the week that I would have something further to say about this resolution today. As hon. members know, the government is hoping that we shall get through on Wednesday afternoon. In some respects the house has not made quite the progress this week that we had hoped it might make; in other respects we have done perhaps even better than we had expected. I think I should allow the motion to stand until Tuesday. By that time it will be possible to know definitely whether we can afford to adjourn on Wednea-day afternoon. I may say that if it appears reasonably certain that we can complete by Wednesday afternoon such essential business as I shall now indicate, the motion will be amended so as to read that when the house adjourns on Wednesday, March 24, it shall stand adjourned until Monday, April 5.
The Minister of Finance has authorized me to say that provision will be made in the supplementary estimates for members' travelling expenses to and from their homes, as has been provided for other short recesses during the past few years. Those who find it more convenient to travel by air will be entitled to do so. [DOT]
I wish now to indicate what remains to be covered between now and the close of Wednesday afternoon if we are to adjourn at that time. If we are not through by Wednesday at six o'clock we shall have to sit, I think, on Wednesday night and possibly also on Thursday. There are amendments to the wheat act. That will be the first item taken up this afternoon. Then there is the Agricultural Products Act which has to go through different stages; then amendments to the emergency tax legislation, covering amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the Customs Act, including the imposition of new taxes and the removal of the old ones.
These have all been mentioned before. I am not certain that I said anything definite about supply. The Minister of Finance did make some reference thereto. Therq are some supplementary estimates to be brought down for the present fiscal year with the resulting supply bill, and then there will be an interim supply bill.
In regard to the supplementary estimates, I would say that so far 'as discussion on these is concerned the government will expect naturally that there will be some debate, but there will not likely be an item in the supplemen-taries that will not be paralleled by what appears in the general estimates, under which discussion on parallel items could take place later on. speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock yesterday it was not expected that this matter would be further dealt with that day. After we left the chamber-and I wish to compliment the government and the house on the plans that were made-provision was made to permit the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) to make his remarks. I believe the leader of the house at that time is to be commended for making it possible for the hon. member, who could not be here today, to make his speech. I understand further that some provision was made to permit me to continue today the remarks I had commenced before six o'clock yesterday, and I want to thank the hon. members responsible for the provision they then made. I do not expect that my remarks today will take more than fifteen minutes, and as far as I am aware this will be the last contribution from this side of the house at this stage of this measure.
When we rose at six o'clock yesterday I was in the midst of discussing the four main features of this bill: first, the pension plan; second, a further payment to the farmers of their own money; third, the proposed power for the board to handle wheat products as well as wheat; and fourth, the compulsory requirement that farmers must sell their oats and barley to the wheat board and no one else.
I had pointed out that we supported the principle of pensions for the employees, but that we were opposed to making the farmers pay half the cost. I had stated that we favoured the government paying the farmers a large part of the farmers' money, which has been withheld from them. I suggest now that when added to the initial payment of $1.35 the total, if possible, should be equal to the present parity price of wheat, which today is about $1.80. Even though the amount on hand is large there may not be enough to bring the payments up to that amount, but if there is not enough the payment should be as large as possible, approaching as nearly as possible the figure I have mentioned.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I had indicated that the expansion of the measure to provide that the board shall handle wheat products as well as wheat was not a very great expansion, and that it had some measure of merit but also that there was some opposition. I suggest that when we get into committee the minister elaborate that point further.
I had indicated also that we are opposed to compelling the owners of oats and barley to sell those products only to the wheat board, thus denying them the right to sell anywhere else if they wish to do so.
In expanding upon these points separately I stated with respect to the pensions proposal that we favoured it in principle; that we saw no reason to object to the employees paying half the cost of their pensions, but that as long as the board is being used for the purposes of the government we were opposed to the farmers being forced to pay half the cost of those pensions. I stated that the imposition upon the farmers of the burden of half the cost of this pension scheme raised a basic question, namely whether this was a farmers' board or a government board. If it is a farmers' board the farmers might reasonably be expected' to bear half the cost of the pensions. If on the other hand it is a government board the government itself should bear that expense, and' it should not be a charge upon the farmers.
The important question before us, therefore, is: whose servant is the wheat board? Is it the servant of the farmers who are compelled to use it, or is it the servant of the government which appoints it and on occasion dictates to it? When the original act was passed in 1935 it was very clear that the wheat board was to sell the farmers' wheat to the best advantage to the farmer in the way of the total price received, the stability of the prices paid the farmer, and the orderly marketing of the product. It was then clearly a board not only designed to function but allowed to function primarily in the interests of the farmers; but it is very clear now that under the present policies of this government the wheat board1 is a government board. It was not only appointed by the government; it is dictated to by the government and is being used by the government for its purposes, not primarily in the interests of the farmers but primarily for the purposes of the government. In carrying out these purposes the government has not hesi.tated- to sell the farmers' product on occasion at less than it might have been sold for. As far as oats and barley are concerned, I predict that the board will be selling them at less than they could be sold for if
the board is given a monopoly in the handling of these products. Under these conditions we say the government, not the farmers, should pay that portion of the cost of the pension scheme which is not paid by the employees themselves.
The second feature of this bill gives the board power to pay back to the farmers at least a part of their own money. It carries out in part, after much delay, what we have urged from the beginning in this matter. From the beginning we favoured a larger initial payment than $1.35 per bushel. But that was not done. From the beginning we favoured paying participation certificates at the end of each year. That was not done. We are opposed to the government holding back large sums of the farmers' money. But the government has held them back. The government is now said to have in its possession some S230 million of the farmers' money.
The government, after long delay, now plans to give back part of this money that it is holding back. It does not tell us exactly how much. It says it will be an increase in the initial payment. The name does not matter much; the payment is what counts. We are in agreement with the proposed increased payment, whatever its amount. I suggest that with the proposed international wheat agreement in prospect, the figure commonly reported of twenty cents a bushel is not enough. It is not nearly a parity price. We favour the payment of as large an amount as is possible at this time.
As I said a minute ago, the farmers should have an amount that approximates the present parity of $1.80. I am aware that because of our British contract-because of having sold two-thirds of the crop at low prices, probably there is not enough money there to reach that figure at this time. In those circumstances I suggest that a payment out large enough to reach as nearly as possible that figure should be made.
The third feature of the measure is that which proposes to give the board power to handle wheat products as well as wheat. Since the act as it now stands gives the board complete power over wheat, it is no great departure to give it the same powers over wheat products. However there have been some protests against this feature. We see both advantages and disadvantages in it. The board got along without it up until now. As I said a minute ago, we ask the government when in committee to give us more information to justify its position with respect to this aspect of the bill.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

The fourth feature of the bill-and this is the one which has provided the most contention in the house-is that which would force farmers who grow oats and1 barley for sale to sell their products only to the wheat board, and to accept for it prices fixed by that board on the dictation of the government. We favour the wheat board being given power to handle oats and barley to the extent that farmers wish them to do so. But we are opposed to forcing farmers to sell to what has now become a government monopoly, if the farmers do not wish to sell to that institution.
We are opposed to this section of the bill because it compels farmers to sell to the wheat board, and denies them the right .to sell anywhere else. We are opposed to this feature of the bill because we feel it means lower prices to farmers who produce oats and barley for sale.
As I have said, the purpose of the original act in 1935 was to market the farmers' wheat to the best advantage as regards total price stability of payments and orderly marketing. But the government is now using it as a national agency to serve another purpose. It is using it as a price control mechanism more than as an agricultural marketing board. And for that purpose it has sold in the past, and no doubt will sell in the future farmers' products at less than those farmers could get for their products if sold by themselves.
Instead of a price supporting agency, as it was originally intended to be, the government is using the wheat board as a price depressing agency in its plans to regulate price controls or price levels in this country. This is a complete perversion of the original conception of the wheat board act, and on that ground we are therefore opposed to this feature of the measure.
A second and related objection to this compulsory aspect of marketing oats and barley is that farmers are forced to sell to a government board at government fixed prices; they are forced to sell to a board administered by government appointees for the purposes of the government, a board which may not sell the farmers' products for the best prices obtainable. This means a substitution-and I shall use a word which I do not use in any offensive sense at all-this means a substitution of political prices in the place of market prices. And when I refer to political prices I mean prices fixed by a board appointed by the government.
If that practice is carried to its logical conclusion it means the suppression by the government of the normal economic laws of buying and selling. In my judgment, such a policy if continued long enough can have only one end, namely disaster to the wheat board

and damage to the prestige of the co-operatives of this country. The policy of political prices for oats and barley will be just another nail in the coffin of the wheat board. It is this kind of policy that leads to the beginning of the end of that board as a marketing organization for farmers.
It has been suggested in this house that the government does not intend or expect to place oats and barley under the sole jurisdiction of the wheat board. It has been suggested that this is but a political move to influence the Saskatchewan provincial election, a political lifeline to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in his fight against the Premier of Saskatchewan. It has been suggested that this measure is a bit of political strategy brought forward to serve the purposes of a provincial election, rather than to serve the needs of agriculture.
I am not making that charge, Mr. Speaker, but I do wish to say that to the extent that such a suggestion is true this bill is a crude and cruel hoax on an important producing group in this country, those who produce oats and barley for sale. If the government is serious in pressing forward this feature of the bill, then I wish to say that we are against it because we are convinced that it will not serve the best interests of those it affects. If the government is not serious in this matter, then there is all the more reason to vote against it, because farmers should not be deceived by the government's pretending that it may do something, and then not doing it.
To summarize briefly what I have tried to say in these few minutes: We strongly favour the payment out to the farmers of their own money. We see some merit in other features of the bill, but we are opposed to that section of it which forces farmers to sell their oats and barley to a board which may, on the government's dictation, sell their products at less than they can be sold for elsewhere.

Right- Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion since I entered the House of Commons in 1935 that I have ever spoken on the subject of wheat. Perhaps I should follow the example of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and give my credentials for doing so.
It seems to be accepted in the. house that any member representing a seat between Whitemouth, Manitoba, and the Rocky mountains, is automatically an expert on wheat marketing. I come from Port Arthur, so perhaps I have to justify my position.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
May I say that I came to western Canada in 1913 as engineer in charge of construction of terminal elevators for the board of grain commissioners. From 1913 to 1935 I spent my time in the company of wheat men. During the intervening years I discussed very little except the marketing of wheat and grain. I have been retained by every farm organization in western Canada that has an investment in terminal elevators, including the early co-operatives and the western wheat pools. I have been retained by considerably more than fifty p.er cent of the private terminal elevator interests of Canada. I have had clients who traded on every major wheat market in the world. Therefore I suggest that if I am not qualified to speak about wheat, I have been collecting fees from clients for a great many years under false pretenses.
I should like for a moment to touch on the subject of pensions for the employees of the wheat board. I cannot believe that there is serious opposition to this measure, or any substance to the suggestion that the salaries of the employees should be paid by the board, and pensions out of the consolidated funds of Canada. We all know that pensions are equivalent to salaries. The proposed pension plan will be about equivalent to a seven per cent increase in the salaries of the employees of the wheat board. The number of employees to be covered by the pension plan is 457. The total number of employees is 686. but of those 229 cannot be included in the scheme because some are under age, some have been employed for periods of less than one year, and some have reached the retirement age. The cost to the board, based on paying one-half of the 14 per cent required for the plan, will amount to 878.400 per year.
It has been suggested that the farmers of Canada will object to having this money paid from the funds of the wheat board. May I say that every farmers' co-operative has a pension plan and the pensions are paid for, as are the salaries of the employees, from the funds of the farmers who own the co-operatives. Practically every grain firm on the Winnipeg grain exchange has a pension plan for its employees. I presume that the revenue of those firms is derived from the wheat farmers just as the revenues of the wheat board are derived from handling the wheat of the farmers.
It was suggested during the debate that the wheat board is overstaffed and overpaid. I find no evidence of that in examining the position of the wheat board. I believe it is a compact organization with a hard-working staff. I know that the salaries, at least of the senior employees, are less than many of
those employees received from the private firms that employed them previously. I suggest that the viewpoint of the farmer is being misrepresented by statements that he would object to the payment of these pensions. I have found that the farmer is as fair an employer as is any other employer in this country, and I speak with some experience. The farmer expects to pay a fair price for efficient service, and in this case I believe he will be glad to see the employees of the wheat board protected by a pension plan.
Then we come to the matter of the increase in the initial payment. There has been a good deal of criticism about the method of marketing wheat and the price received by the farmer. Various controversial statements about marketing have been made. It seems to me that this criticism overlooks entirely the situation of trading in wheat in the world today. Practically all wheat, in fact I think I can say all wheat, is sold from government to government. In other words, state marketing is practically universal at the present time.
Several speakers have mentioned a world price for wheat. I suggest that there is no such thing. There are no international exchanges doing business today as there were in pre-war days. In pre-war days there was a definite world price for wheat. If one market was out of line, another market would sell wheat into it until prices were equalized. Where are the markets today? The Winnipeg grain exchange, one of the great pre-war markets, is closed to wheat trading. The Bolsa in Buenos Aires is closed to wheat trading. The Baltic in London is closed to wheat trading. The Liverpool corn exchange is closed. The markets of Europe are all closed, as are the markets of Australia. Where in the world can a world price for wheat be found when there is no world trading in wheat?
I was interested in looking up the prices being charged in state marketing on a given date. Argentina was selling wheat to various countries at prices ranging up to $5 per bushel. Australia was selling wheat under a one year contract to the United Kingdom at $2.72 per bushel and to India at $2.98 per bushel. Chicago May futures closed on that date at $2.45|. Canada's class 2 price on that day stood at $2.75. Those prices represent the major world trading today, and where in that collection can you find a world price?
It will be said that the United States markets are still open. They are the only markets in the world that I know of that are trading in wheat today. But I would point

Canadian Wheat Board Act
out that there is a difference between trading in international wheat and trading in domestic wheat. Canadian wheat cannot be shipped into United States markets because present customs tariffs provide for an entry of only 800,000 bushels of wheat per annum from Canada into the United States. Sales abroad are not made from United States markets. The only wheat that the United States is shipping is wheat bought by a government agency and shipped by that government agency. The Chicago price is a domestic price. We all know that speculation on that market grew to such an extent that it became a national scandal. The President of the United States denounced it, and the Secretary of Agriculture denounced it. The names of traders on the exchange were published. They numbered more than 3,000 large and small traders who were buying and selling wheat that they never had owned and never expected to own.
However, the Chicago market price is arrived at freely by buyer and seller and Canada has used it as a guide for its No. 2 wheat price. The No. 2 price is the United States price corrected for the higher protein value of Canadian wheat. The price arrived at in that way can hardly be called a world price, and I hope hon. members will not continue to refer to it as a world price. It is nothing more than the Chicago price corrected for protein content.

Some of your colleagues have done the same thing. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) used the expression "political prices" in place of market prices, and he also mentioned sales in the interests of the farmer. What are the interests of the farmer? The interests of the farmer are to have a sure market, a stable market and a price that is fair. It is easy to find spot markets that will offer higher prices. Starving people, if they have money at all, are not in position to question the price that may be charged for the food they must have. That is why Argentina is able to sell its wheat up to $5 per bushel.
However, Canada has a special responsibility in a time like this. We are far and away the largest wheat exporting country in the world. We have a particular responsibility to our largest customer, the United Kingdom. Over the years the United Kingdom has been the country upon which Canada has depended to buy a large part of our exportable surplus of wheat. When war broke out Canada assumed the responsibility of seeing that the United Kingdom was supplied with wheat

from this country. For a time it was sent as a gift, and later it was sent as mutual aid. The government felt that it was the continuing responsibility of Canada to see that Britain was supplied with wheat during the reconstruction period and at a price which Britain could consider reasonable. Therefore a four-year contract was made. That contract was submitted to the House of Commons, and I would remind hon. gentlemen that every member of the House of Commons voted in favour of ratifying that contract. It is well to keep that in mind when that contract is being discussed in this house. It is every hon. member's contract as well as the government's contract.

I believe that that contract has worked out decidedly in the best interests of the farmers of western Canada. Today Canada has a place firmly established in the British loaf of bread. Today we are supplying 60 per cent of the wheat that goes into the British loaf. I remember that after a rather unpleasant difference with the United Kingdom in 1930 the position of Canada in the British loaf dropped as low as 20 per cent. I believe that Britain feels that Canada has treated her fairly in setting the current price for wheat. The price for the 1948-49 crop has been agreed on at $2 a bushel, and it is interesting to note that the three great

Canadian Wheat Board Act
exporting countries of the world, meeting in Washington a few weeks ago. decided that the importing countries thought $2 was a fair maximum price for wheat to continue over the next five-year period.
It has been suggested in this house that the farmer is the only producer in Canada who has not been getting the last cent out of his product that could be obtained. That suggestion is entirely unrealistic. Let me discuss prices of one or two other basic products. Let us take newsprint as an example, the second largest export commodity in Canada. Newsprint is very like wheat in that it is produced from the natural products of Canada and it is largely sold in the world markets. I asked our export department to give me their opinion of the world price of newsprint over the last three or four years, and I was told that it ranged somewhere between $200 and $300 a ton. I know that I have had a good many callers from overseas and from the United States to ask for an allocation, saying that they were willing to pay up to $300 a ton for newsprint.

speechtext:
There is a world market for wheat but no world price for wheat. I am giving the opinion of my officers as to what newsprint could have been sold for had the Canadian -producers agreed to go out for the last cent they could get out of the newsprint.
What is the history up to the beginning of this year? No producer in Canada had ever charged more than $90 a ton for his newsprint. So far as I know there has never been a ton of newsprint shipped to the grey market or shipped to an unofficial market. The newsprint industry has believed it is wise to ship newsprint to their traditional customers and to price that newsprint at prices which the customer could afford to pay. The record indicates rather remarkable restraint. I think that the businessmen who operate cur newsprint industry are able, wise and far-seeing. I have heard my hon. friends of the C.C.F.
party refer to these same men as greedy monopolists. However, that has been the policy of these men. They have believed that it was better to protect a sure market and a continuing market for their newsprint, better to keep their customers solvent, and to keep relations good rather than to go after the last immediate dollar that they could get for that product. That is one analogy with the farmers' position. I would point out also that the newsprint manufacturers have always quoted a lower price to Canadian customers than they have quoted to their foreign customers.
Let us take another analogy. Let us take lumber. When the controls of lumber were lifted there were three prices for lumber. I am taking west coast lumber as an example. The Canadian price was $29 a thousand; the price to the United .Kingdom was $60 a thousand and the price to the United States and to other spot markets was $87 a thousand. There again the lumber producer was protecting his domestic market because of ceiling prices, but hon. members will notice that he was also protecting his United Kingdom market by quoting prices that were only about two-thirds of world prices for lumber. Therefore let it not be said again that the farmer has been placed in a special position through the policy of selling his product to a continuing customer at a reasonable price, and a price that that customer would not consider a hold-up.
Reference was made to extending the control of wheat to wheat products. This is necessary to insure that all wheat used in domestic consumption returns to the five-year pool the full current price. Any system which permitted the miller to pay less than full current prices would mean that the amounts available to go to increase initial payment from the five-year pool would be short to that extent. I hardly think it is necessary to dwell on that point.
We come now to the section bringing the marketing of oats and barley under the control of the wheat board. I made a lengthy statement setting out the government's views of this section when I introduced the resolution preceding the bill. The government fully appreciates the difficulty of the course that is opening up in this direction, but it does feel that at the moment there is an overwhelming demand from the farmers of this country that the marketing of oats and barley be placed under the board. The government may be wrong in this, but I see no indication of it.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) suggested that the Alberta wheat pool did not favour this course, and I am placing
Canadian Wheat Board Act

this telegram from Ben Plumer, president of the pool, on Hansard because the telegram requests that I do so. It reads as follows:
Apparently as a result of certain discussions which took place at the annual meeting of Canadian Federation of Agriculture held in Brockvdlle the latter part of January respecting the marketing of coarse grains the Winnipeg Free Press has persistently inferred in a series of editorial comments in their column as well as in certain news dispatches originating with their Ottawa correspondent that the Alberta wheat pool in some way has dissociated itself from other farm organizations in their demands on the federal government that the marketing of coarse grain be taken over by a government body. We also understand from press dispatches of earlier this week that the member for West Calgary, Mr. A. L. Smith, in his speech to the House of Commons in opposition to all coarse grains being marketed by the Canadian wheat board for a government body, indicated that our association was not favourable to coarse grains being handled in this manner. It is not quite true in the discussions at Brockville that our representatives expressed doubt as to the advisability of pressing the federal government to have the marketing of coarse grains handled by the Canadian wheat board in view of their present heavy responsibilities in respect to the marketing of wheat, flax and oil seeds and suggested a separate coarse grains board as an alternative. In accordance with our position as already outlined to you by our manager, Mr. R. D. Purdy, in a personal interview with you when in Ottawa some days ago, this will confirm that the Alberta wheat pool has consistently supported over the past several years, in conjunction rvith other farm organizations, the principle that all coarse grains should be marketed through a government board. We would ask that you arrange for this message to be read into Hansard as a means of definitely clearing up any doubt that our association has at all times consistently supported the principle that the marketing of all coarse grains should be placed under a federal government board and any statements or suggestions to the contrary are not in accordance with the facts.
Ben S. Plumer, Chairman,
Alberta Wheat Pool.
I have a somewhat similar wire from Roy C. Marler, president of the Alberta federation of agriculture, which I am not going to take the time to read.
I think that covers the remarks I have to make. It has been stated to me that I would have as much of this day to discuss wheat as seemed necessary for the purpose, but that if the bill failed to pass today it would have to hold over until after the Easter recess. That would mean more than two weeks' delay in getting out the cheques the farmers need to pay for their seeding expense. Therefore I hope that we can press

this measure through and send it on its way before eleven o'clock this evening.

speechtext:
On several occasions the minister in charge of this bill and the Minister of Agriculture have stated that there is no such thing as a world price for wheat today. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed that out this afternoon. Some time
ago, during another debate, I put on the record a clause from the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. This clause will be found on page 658 of Hansard and reads:
In determining the actual price in the last two years regard will be had to the extent to which the agreed price for the first two years falls below the world price for that period. Our farmers are therefore protected from crippling losses should there be a world slump in wheat prices. This is the commercial advantage which Canada secures.
A year ago the then minister of trade and commerce gave all credit to the Minister of Agriculture for having negotiated this agreement and being partly responsible for its drafting. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture would take advantage of this opportunity to tell us what is meant by the words "world price" in the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. I am wondering why those words were inserted in that agreement for the protection of the farmer when there is no such thing as a world price today?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I dealt with that matter before the Christmas recess and gave an explanation. The term "world price" as used there is, as we explained a few moments ago, based on the United States price, the Chicago price. In the real sense of the term it is the domestic United States price, but it was the only price that was established on any market in the world. What the minister said a few moments ago is perfectly true; there is no world price in the generally accepted meaning of the term.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Is it fair to assume that in negotiating the price for wheat in 1948 and 1949 the United States price will be the one used in the negotiations so far as the Canadian officials are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: It is fair to assume that consideration will be given to the relationship of the United States price with the price obtained from Britain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
There seems to have been considerable dissension about the phrase "world price". I would be quite satisfied to use the words "class 2 wheat price" instead of world price. That term would be better understood by the farmers of the prairie provinces. If they can get the price being obtained for class 2 wheat I do not think there will be any further dissension.
In closing the debate a few moments ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that Canada has a special responsibility. I think we all agree with the minister in that respect, but we do not agree that that responsibility should be borne only by the wheat growers of
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the prairie provinces. That has been our objection since the British wheat agreement was made. I repeat that we have no objection to the low price being paid by the people of Britain for this wheat, but we do insist that that is a responsibility of all the people of Canada, not one for the farmers alone.
Dealing further with the $2 maximum price for the next five-year period, I am not prepared to agree that that is just because we have not before us the terms of the agreement. I hope to have something more to say about this. When the minister made the announcement he said that that maximum price would hold good, regardless of the cost of production. While the price of wheat is controlled, while there is a maximum price on wheat, other things should not be allowed to go uncontrolled. It may be just one more bad deal being foisted on the farmers of this country. When we get to the coarse grains I hope to have a little more to say, but I wanted to say this much in connection with the wheat question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

speechtext:

Canadian Wheat Board Act
board. I wish to read a telegram I received from the Great Star milling company in the county of Perth:
Understand bill 136 is under consideration and section 27 giving the wheat board control over wheat and wheat products. If board control wheat products this will mean the milling industry will be subject to complete control of board. This is giving a board powers that only the government itself should assume and then only in times of emergency. Strongly urge utmost opposition to including wheat products or grain products in this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: If this section passes, all products of grain crossing a provincial boundary will be subject to the control of the board. The reason for that is that it touches on the point raised by the hon. member for Calgary West. This is a five-year pool. The price next year, we know, will be high and there may be a temptation for certain farmers to by-pass the pool and deliver to mills, instead of waiting to get the participation in the pool, taking immediate cash, in an amount which may be higher than the final result of the pool. That miller will probably have an advantage over millers who buy wheat from the wheat board, and the pool would not be getting all the revenue that is coming to it. The wheat board tell me that this provision is necessary at the present stage of the pool, and therefore I am asking the House of Commons to pass it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

give board powers greatly disproportionate to the purpose it is trying to effect. Milling industry already working under severe handicaps and believe it would be discriminatory and not in the national policy to put industry under complete government control as is outlined in bill 135,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

Any products that the governor in council may name. I hardly think they will get down to shredded wheat. My hon. -friend says that the millers have been discriminated against and are under a severe handicap.
I just suggest that the government has been putting wheat in their mills at a standard price, selling their products in foreign markets and giving them a good margin. I think the hardship they have suffered will be reflected in their earnings over that period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: In addition to that, can the minister tell us what is permitted under the regulations? subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The regulations are not as yet drawn, and it is difficult to say what will be in them. Canadian Wheat Board Act

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Why bother, then?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I want to ask the minister one simple question. I am much impressed, as I hear him talk, as to the position of the milling and other industries. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: State marketing is socialism, yes, if you like. But it is hard to be different in a world that at the moment is following state marketing for reasons which I think are largely beyond their control. There are currency problems, credit problems and a number of factors, which are driving countries to state marketing at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I think there are such factors, just as the minister says. But a good deal depends, in the last analysis, on what we want to do right here in our own hearts. I understand that the minister has agreed that this is a highly socialistic measure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: A moment ago the minister said no regulations had been drawn. In this section 27, paragraph (b) and the following ones "wheat or wheat products" are the words used. It is always "wheat or wheat products". The regulations are in existence under which wheat has been handled. I would ask the minister whether those same regulations are the ones which it is proposed to enforce here or whether a completely new set of regulations will be drawn up as far as flour, mill feeds and so on are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely some plans have been made as to what those regulations will be. The minister cannot be entirely without any knowledge of what the regulations will be, and how they will differ from the regulations now in force as far as wheat itself is concerned. If there is to be any difference, I do not think we should give the government a blank cheque to make any regulations they like in order to handle these things afterwards. We should have some knowledge here as to what those regulations are, what the government will be able to do under them, how they will affect the ordinary people and the ordinary millers. From what the minister has stated so far, we have no idea how the thing will affect
{Mr. Howe.]
the people most concerned, and I think those are matters on which we should get information before we pass the section.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

I do not suppose the bill can be divided at this point. But, in respect of oats and barley, I cannot for the life of me understand this House of Commons, in view of the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that the handling of oats and barley is unconstitutional. He argued that himself in the resolution stage of the measure. Other people who should know have pointed out that enabling legislation from every province in Canada would be required before this could be made operative. That would apply not only to the three prairie provinces which produce oats and barley. I understand from those trained in the law-and they should know-that the same type of legislation would be required from other provinces where this oats or barley may be traded. This would mean that each of the nine provinces in Canada would require that legislation.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I thought I had protested this as strongly as I could. The minister introduced the legislation and argued, himself, that it was unconstitutional until such legislation was provided. The Minister of Justice certainly felt that it was unconstitutional, and said on repeated occasions that the law officers of the crown had advised that it was unconstitutional.
Why in the world would a government introduce a measure like that, knowing that it is unconstitutional at this time, and without referring it to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for at least some study?
We do not want to appear as foolish as that in the eyes of the people of this country, or to people of other countries. That does not seem to make common sense at all, in the matter of legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that the bill as it is drafted today is quite constitutional. There is a limitation on the power that the government can exercise under the bill. subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

We are passing enabling legislation which, so far as this measure goes, will permit us to do all we legally can do. In saying that, I repeat that our powers are'not sufficient, and this bill is not sufficient to organize a compulsory pool on wheat and barley that would succeed. What others do is the responsibility of others.
It may be that we shall have sufficient legislation passed in those proper jurisdictions to enable the pool to be worked out. If that is so, the government has done its part, and will be ready to act. We will make sure that others have taken the necessary steps to permit the operation of the pool within their jurisdictions. We will also make sure that both sellers and buyers, so far as they are organized farmers, are also satisfied that the combined legislation will permit a workable arrangement, and that a pattern for operating the pool can be worked out satisfactorily to both.

I should like to speak to the minister about oats and barley. I have received a lot of correspondence lately with respect to this matter, including a file which the Minister of Finance knows all about, because I have been sent copies of the correspondence that was exchanged with him. I am not going to read it, first, because it is too long and, second, because the last letter contains a reference to myself. With my usual modesty I just could not have that become public property.
It is a fact that today in Canada we have a large surplus of oats and barley. If anyone is interested I have all the figures here of what is at the head of the lakes and at the lake ports. In various parts of the country there will be new grains of this type coming on to the markets everywhere. It is said that at the present time there are bids in the market from the United States, Eire, Belgium, the Scandinavian countries and Holland, with payment in United States dollars and at prices higher than can be got for the grains in this country. In short they say that this is a matter, possibly of great urgency; that unless this surplus which amounts to-I shall put it very low-30,000,000 bushels is taken care of, unless it is channeled off for useful purposes, it will lie there against what is at present maintained west of the lakes. It is contended that immediately navigation opens there will be trouble, to say nothing of what will take place when the new crop comes on.
I am taking this opportunity of saying to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has been known to act quickly in times gone by-
Canadian Wheat Board Act

it is one of his most admirable qualities among many-that this matter should be looked into immediately. If the information I have been given is correct, it indicates a serious condition in western Canada. I am not going to say any more than that. I am sure, from the various sources of information which I have and which I think are accurate, that this is a matter which needs correcting. The minister can, by one swift move, eliminate this top-heavy thing which is rolling around on top of our market. He can do that by loosening up on export permits. We do not need to put ourselves in danger, but in this correspondence there are a number of letters from Ontario and Quebec cancelling orders. In fact today feed is just not moving. That is an unusual condition at this time of the year. Everyone seems to be saying that he is well stocked up.
I am merely asking the minister to look into this matter because it seems to those of us who are amateurs, who have not his knowledge from the various sources of information he has, that this is a serious condition. There is a possibility that I am overstating it, but I am quite sure I am not to any great degree. If what I have said is correct, I think it is something the minister might well look into in the course of the next few days.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise to a matter of privilege if Your Honour will permit me to do so, in order to make a correction in last week's debate on insurance. I do so for the purpose of setting the record straight. There was a good deal of questioning as to what the Saskatchewan benefits really were, and I have here a very short paragraph which I desire to read1 in order to complete the record and ensure that no misunderstandings were left in the matter. It will take only a minute.
I have a letter from the minister of social welfare, Hon. 0. W. Valleau, of Saskatchewan, which reads in part as follows:
Public liability and property damage insurance of $5,000 injury to one person in one accident, $10,900 injury to two or more persons in one accident, and $1,000 property damage. This is what is known as standard liability and property damage insurance, and is the type required under the liability laws in force I believe in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario as well as some thirty-eight states in the United States. The insurance on all ears when they are outside of the province of Saskatchewan will be standard in every particular, but on cars inside the province the property damage of $1,000 will be subject to a deductible of $100. This is to bring it in line with our collision insurance and also to relieve us of the administrative task of being involved in every accident on 170,000 to 180,000 vehicles where the damage is less than $100 in extent, no changes being made in the rates which, as you will recall, were $4.50 for cars under 111-inch wheel base, and $6.00 for those over, with varying rates for trucks, buses, et cetera.
I simply wash to put that question right. The other benefits regarding hospitalization, medical attention or funeral benefits and1 so on are as I stated them last week.

Let me say again that I am in agreement with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), and I know that other members in the house, in various quarters, are of the same view, that these huge public utilities should be publicly owned. Whatever our differences of opinion may be on private enterprise, I believe there is a considerable body of opinion in all parts for the public ownership of public utilities in order that they may be properly regulated with a view to giving proper rates and service to the community.
Moreover, the Bell Telephone Company is a very important company in our own country, for this company owns more telephone lines in the country, and has a larger number of subscribers than all the rest of the telephone companies in the country including the three publicly owned telephone systems in the prairie provinces. These three are owned, of course, by the provincial governments, and as I said on a former occasion they give excellent service, and incidentally encounter many more hazards and difficulties than a telephone system which is serving more or less congested areas. Yet they are able to make substantial returns to the provinces and at the same time, as I shall show in a moment, give the users of those telephone systems cheaper rates than are provided in this part of the country by the Bell Telephone Company.
I should point out, too, that the Bell Telephone Company is controlled by a large corporation in the United States. It is, I believe, controlled in part by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and therefore may be considered to be a subsidiary of that great

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because a great increase in capital is being asked for by the Bell Telephone Company. I have no quarrel with that company. I have been acquainted and connected with all its personnel in the city of Toronto, and I have 
found them to be fine, outstanding men. The employees must live up to certain standards. The executives take part in every worthy work in that city. I know they engage in a great deal of research work, and are all the time trying to find out what the necessities of the future will be as far as telephones are concerned. In that way they acquire a great deal of knowledge which they have always placed at the disposal, free of charge, of any worthy cause or any municipal or other body. Therefore I say I have only the kindliest feelings toward the Bell Telephone Company.
Nor do I intend to complain particularly about their rates as far as the city of Toronto is concerned. I think those rates are very fair. That may not be entirely true as far as the suburbs of Toronto are concerned, and I think that is where the main objection comes from. The city of Toronto covers a very large area, and from time to time the telephone company has extended its basic area to include not only the city itself but the township of York, with some 85,000 people, and the township of East York, with another 45,000. So that from time to time, perhaps as a result of a little pressure from the municipalities, the basic area has been extended. In the last few years the suburbs have grown tremendously; and many people in those districts which have been built up during the war and since are complaining of the higher rates they have to pay, and urging that they should be included with those who enjoy the basic rate. That is, of course, a matter which can be threshed out before the board of transport commissioners.
However I do object to the Bell Telephone Company coming here at this time and asking for an increase of $350,000,000 in their capital. That is a sizeable amount and, as far as I can see, it has not been justified by anything presented by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) in sponsoring this bill. The hon. member gave the house information which I have read. I have read, as well, the financial statement of the company for 1946, to which I shall refer a little later. I say I do not see any justification at all for this application. When this company was incorporated in 1880 it was given powers about as extensive as it could think of at that time, though those powers may not be so extensive now as the company would wish, because of new inventions which have come along. At that time the company started with a capitalization of $500,000. Some time later this was increased to $50,000,000, and eventually, in 1927, the company was allowed to increase its capital to $150,000,000.
As far as I can learn, as late as 1945 the company had used only $35,000,000 of this

______________Bell Telephone Company
increased capital. In other words, in 1945 the issued capital of the telephone company was only $85,000,000, and, after all, in 1945 they were serving a very large number of people. We must remember that this company operates only in Ontario and Quebec; and from the remarks of the hon. member sponsoring the bill we have learned that there are about 1,300,000 telephones in use. Even allowing for the fact that there are a great many business telephones, the number of other users cannot be increased very greatly unless the company goes into outside districts; and here again I want to corroborate to some extent what was said by the last speaker. I do not think the Bell Telephone Company is anxious to go outside the cities and larger centres of population. In other places there is a municipal, township or county telephone system which provides service for the local people, with perhaps as many as twenty-two on a line, and the Bell Telephone provides a long distance connection with that line. These people are quite satisfied; they get their telephone service quite reasonably, and have the benefit of long distance calls through the Bell Telephone Company and their own connections through their own little company.
I said that up to 1945 only $85,000,000 of the authorized capital of the company had been used. In 1946 this was increased to $86,000,000, and at the end of 1946 it stood at $104,000,000. The sponsor of this bill says that, in the last year or a little more, it has gone up to about $134,000,000. In other words, during the past four years the capital of the company has been increased by $50,000,000 and, as the sponsor says, this has been used to bring about certain improvements and extensions, and to give service to those who could not obtain it previously.
But that is not all the money available to the company. According to the Canada Gazette of very recent date the company has issued notice that it will apply to execute a mortgage bond which will give it another $35,000,000. I do not suppose all this money will become available to the company, because, as I understand these statements, there is a balance of $7,500,000 of a five per cent loan which, I believe, has never been paid off, and probably that will be paid out of this amount. But even so they will have $27,500,000 from this bond issue. They will also have all their free assets. I must admit that their assets are not entirely free, that they consist largely of fixed assets, but still they have some investments. For instance, they have investment securities amounting to $21,000,000, as well as other securities amounting to another
few million dollars. So it is only fair to say that at this moment they have some $40,000,000 with which to go ahead; and that again is a considerable sum of money.
As I have said, the capital issued amounts to $136,000,000 but they have a depreciation reserve of $99,000,000, which ordinarily would be available for maintenance, repairs, improvements and so on. I am afraid, however, that this reserve has probably been used in connection with the fixed assets, to provide new telephones and equipment. But it is in fact there, and it is a nice, sizeable sum of money available to the stockholders, though they cannot use it at the present time.
I say that the amount of money for which they are asking cannot be justified in any way. The hon. member for Outremont who is sponsoring the bill spoke about what has been done in the last two years. I believe he pointed out that between August 1, 1945, and December 1, 1947, the company had installed a total of 293,000 telephones at a cost of $89,300,000. If that is so, those installations must have cost $305 each. Another 89,000 telephones are required, and they should not cost much more, if any, than the $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 the company has available at the present time.
I do not think anyone is so naive as to doubt that if a depression, however small, were to come, a good many telephones would be taken out, and would be available for use somewhere else. As a matter of fact, I believe the business of the Bell Telephone Company is as good an index as can be found of business conditions across the country, because one of the first things a person does if he is in difficulty is to get along without any telephone.
I am not suggesting that one should have to do without telephone service. It is a necessary service; and not just to keep the members of families talking to one another, but so that a businessman may keep in touch with his business, and so that doctors and other people may keep in contact with those for whom they are acting.
I do not want the people of Toronto to have to pay higher rentals for their telephones. The company has got along in the past. It is my belief that, the larger a city becomes, the more the telephone rates should be reduced, because the service is contained in a small area. All that is required under the automatic system is to get more automatic equipment. I know it has happened-in my own experience only once-* that when one tried to get a party on a certain exchange he could not do so because
Bell Telephone Company

the connection was engaged as a result of too many people talking through that exchange. Up to the present time, however, that has happened only once in my experience, and I use the telephone frequently.
If $350 million in stock is issued at a rate of eight per cent it will mean an additional $28,000,000 per year to charge against the service. If that were divided among 1,500,000 subscribers it would mean about $18.65 a year per individual telephone. And, remember this, that you have only a limited number of new subscribers to whom telephone service may be extended and in the number of subscribers above I am adding on 200,000 to the telephones which are now in use. I feel certain that, if this great expenditure is permitted the cost to owner and user is bound to be increased.
Is it necessary for the Bell Telephone Company to sell more stock? Let me say that while they have been a satisfactory company, so far as their business methods are concerned, yet in one sense they are the greatest monopoly one could possibly imagine. There can be two railway companies; there can be two street railway systems; there can be two gas companies-two of almost anything else. But there cannot be two telephone systems operating in the same area, because, in my younger days, I lived in a town where there were two systems, and the result was that one had to have both installations. For satisfaction, you have to have telephone connections with all other telephone users.
In this instance, therefore, the Bell Telephone Company has the greatest of all monopolies. Perhaps its only justification for its existence lies in the fact that, like the gas company in Toronto, this telephone company has operated well, and at least to my satisfaction. I know nothing bad about it.
But, after all, they have a monopoly. They are really trustees for the people. If it became a question of whether the Bell Telephone Company should operate privately, or under government control, at the present time I would choose the private company, on account of the manner in which it has operated. But, after all, they are operating their company to make money, and they must be stopped. No, I shall say they must be controlled, not stopped, because human nature is too strong to resist making more money, if there is an opportunity to do so.
I do not think this parliament of Canada, at this particular time of all times, should consent to such a large increase in capital. It would1 tie the hands of succeeding parliaments, and we do not know what lies in the future.

I do not believe we have any right to make that commitment. It may be said that this matter will go before the board of transport commissioners. That, of course, is a fact. But, after all, we are the body who are responsible to the people. We are the governing bodjr responsible for this matter, although we have not had a great deal of opportunity lately to carry out our wishes in a democratic way. I still think, however, that at this particular time we cannot give up rights which we have, nor can we abuse the trust the people have placed in us.
May I say a word about television. I believe television is a reality of the future, and something which may be of importance to the people. I do not know how it will develop, nor do I know who will produce it. I do not think, however, that the Bell Telephone Company should use funds made available for the operation of the telephone system for purposes of developing television.
I cannot think of anyone who wants television badly. Certainly I do not; I have no great desire to see the person to whom I am talking. It might be all right, but if it is to cost a hundred million dollars or a hundred and fifty million dollars, we can quite well do without it. I suggest that if television is to come in, and if the Bell Telephone Company is interested in it, then it should operate through a subsidiary, and the money the people pay in for a telephone service should be used for that service alone.
If the stock is offered on the market it cannot very well be offered at $100 a share. I believe the average price obtained from new stock issued over the years has been considerably higher than that, running up to $130 or $140. At present I believe it is being sold to employees of the company at $145.
There are many of the original shareholders who still own their own stock. The sponsor of the bill has said that the American telephone company owns fourteen per cent of the stock; I thought it was more, but I suppose it is a fact that, as the stock increases in amount their percentage decreases. That is quite right. I believe a short time ago it was as high as twenty per cent, but as stock is sold their percentage increases. The American telephone company are still holding stock that they bought at $100 a share. So that in any event, where stock is sold at more than its par value it means that they get the benefit to that extent. I should think that after sixty-seven years, since the original stock was sold, they could well do without getting any increase in

Bell Telephone Company
the value of their stock by new stock being offered to the public at less than market value.
I am strongly opposed to section 3 of the bill, which splits the present stock in four parts. I know the Bell Telephone Company do not want it, and it is to their credit that they do not. I can recall when one large organization in Toronto divided its stock into a four-to-one split. The stock went up in a bull market to such an extent that the one-fourth share sold for as much as the old original share. I cannot conceive of anyone wanting to buy a share of stock who cannot pay S100 for it. I think it is our duty to see that this stock is not cut up. I think it is just a stock selling proposition.
I am glad to see that the company has clarified to some extent the situation in connection with stock bequeathed by wills, and I believe that a transfer office has been opened in Toronto in addition to the office in Montreal. If that is not true, I think it should be done. It is not fair that people who own stock in a company which is at least one-half an Ontario company should have to go to Montreal in another province to have stock transferred.
I think the Bell Telephone Company should modify their bill. If all this stock is issued it will mean that they have a capitalization equal to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If they get in all this money they will actually have more money than the Ontario Hydro Electric system has now or will have when recent developments are completed. They are really asking for something that no one can foresee they will ever need. I do not think they have a right to come here and ask us to vote to approve their request.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring out a few points in this debate. From what I can learn, the company has $20,000,000 left and it wants $350,000,000 more. I like speaking in those terms, because in the past I was always in the nickel and dime class. Seemingly we are now dealing in astronomical figures. With this $350 million this company could absorb all the remaining privately or publicly owned telephone systems in Canada and become a monopoly. Perhaps the greatest weakness in the system of free enterprise is the constant tendency to go into monopoly. I would think that hon. members on the Liberal side would be quite sensitive about this and try to protect the people from this form of economy.
When monopolies such as this grow to such an extent they wipe out the small businessman and become what we term a soulless and heartless machine. During the war the army built
a telephone line between Prince Rupert and Jasper for its own use. After the war that was taken over by the public works department. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation pipe in a few programs over that line, but not all. If they piped in all their programs the Department of Public Works would charge so much that they could not afford it. The public works department said that they were giving a figure which was comparable with what a privately owned company would charge, and when they said that they were talking about only one company, and this is it.
Another interesting feature is that, while all the programs of the C.B.C. are constantly going over that wire, they charge only for those which are broadcast. I assume that the rest are run down the sewer, simply piped to one side. That is what you are up against when you try to get something for people in outlying parts of the world. You are met with the statement., "This is what private industry would1 charge." I submit that private industry as represented by this company dominates the whole picture in Canada today.
I suppose if one were to look at it from a cynical point of view or a non-constructive point of view he would let such bills as this run their course, so that the thing would become so transparent to the people that they would solve their problem by putting in a socialist government. Actually the people of Canada are becoming only too aware of such companies as this, and it is such things that are causing a political awakening of the people.	.
Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, there are two features that have given me some concern in connection with this bill, and I should like to draw them to the attention of the hon. member for Outre-mont (Mr. Rinfret) who is sponsoring the bill. The first has to do with the question of rates. In the press of February 26 there appeared a dispatch from Montreal headed, "Hints of increase in telephone rates", which read as follows:
Frederick Johnson, president of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, told the annual meeting today that the company "cannot live forever within its present rates for service."
We had some experience in the house last year in connection with a bill brought in by the British Columbia Telephone Company. At that time I asked the sponsor, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), the intentions of the company with regard to rates. I should like to quote from page 2718

of Hansard of May 2, 1947, just to show the house what was said at that time. I asked the hon. member:
In this case, where there is a big increase in capital-
At that time we thought it was quite a big increase, but it was only from $11,000,000 to $25,000,000, which was small change compared with the increase asked for in the present bill.
-I think it is essential that some protection should be given to telephone users of British Columbia. I understand that the hon. member has been authorized to give assurance to the effect that the company has no present intention of applying for an increase of rates and will not make any such application unless compelled to do so by extensive changes in conditions.
Mr. Beid: That is my definite understanding.
Mr. Green:	That assurance is clearly worded
and contains a statement to the effect that an application will not be made unless the company is compelled to do so and then only by reason of extensive changes in conditions. If the hon. member for New Westminster is prepared to give that assurance on behalf of the British Columbia Telephone Company I for one shall have no objection to the bill passing.
Mr. Reid:	I am authorized to do so, and it
is my definite understanding.
I should like to know whether the hon. member for Outremont can give the same assurance on behalf of the Bell Telephone Company. It is important that we know whether or not the company intends, once this bill goes through, to apply for an increase in rates which, of course, will affect thousands and thousands of people and is a very important factor.
The second feature which has given me some concern is the amount of the increase requested, from $150 million to $500 million. By an amendment in 1882 the works of this company were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. I suggest to hon. members that this parliament is responsible for, and should keep in touch with, what is done by the company. For that reason it is important that the company should have to come back to the house every so often. That is one reason why it should not be given an increase that is too large; the result might be that it would not come back here for twenty or thirty years; therefore I do ask the sponsor to give consideration to agreeing to have the amount of increase cut; I do not say to what figure, but I think the company is asking for too much. Last year the British Columbia Telephone Company increased its capital from $11,000,000 to $25,000,000, as I have said; or slightly more than double. Perhaps some such provision would be satisfactory to the Bell Telephone Company.

In speaking on second reading of the bill, the hon. member for Outremont explained that during the next five years it was planned to spend about $362 million. That information will be found at page 1701 of Hansard. Then, on page 1702 he explained that only about half of that amount would be raised by sale of capital. He said the rest of it would be obtained from borrowings and from other available resources of the company. Therefore, to provide for this capital expenditure in the next five years the company obviously does not need to have its capital increased by $350 million.
I would point out that the company has been coming back to the house in years gone by. Perhaps the hon. member for Outremont will correct me if I make a mistake in any of the dates. My understanding is that the company was incorporated in 1880, at which time it was given the power to do certain things. The maximum capital allowed was $1,000,000. In 1884 that was increased to $2,000,000; in 1892 to $5,000,000; in 1902 to $10,000,000; in 1906 to $30,000,000; in 1920 to $75,000,000; in 1929 to $150 million, and in 1948 we have the request for an increase from $150 million to $500 million.
I hope that the hon. member for Outremont will be able to make some statement to the house on these two points; first, as to whether assurance can be given with regard to an application for an increase in rates; second, whether the company would be satisfied to have a smaller increase at the present time. His answer to these two suggestions might make a material difference in the vote of quite a few hon. members.

I rather think we are all out of order, but I think I should be permitted to say something in reference to what has just been stated. As a matter of fact, I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce today went very much farther than he undertook to go when the statement was made. The proposal at that time was that if, by doing so, we could advance the discussion of this measure, he was prepared to move that we instruct the committee to divide this legislation. That proposal in the first instance came from the C.C.F.; and immediately after it was made, members of the official opposition rose in their places and protested, making statements which were interpreted by the house to be in opposition to the proposals made by the minister. As a result of those statements, three members of the C.C.F. group rose one after another and withdrew their support of the suggestion they themselves had previously made that the bill be divided and the oats and barley section be referred to the committee on agriculture.
At that time I rose in my place and tried to suggest to the official opposition that they should accept the proposal of the minister. At no time did they accept it. They went right on discussing the question, and continued to discuss it for, I think, about two days. Then, when the matter came back to the house the discussion was continued, so that I think the minister would have been quite justified in saying today he was under no obligation whatever to go farther with the proposal which was made a few days ago, or what has come to be a few weeks ago. However he took the position that, since some objection was raised by the official opposition
to that suggestion, he would make the motion he had suggested he would make. That motion was moved; the house was given an opportunity to divide on it; it did divide, and the result of the division was a denial of the suggestion made, not by the official opposition but in the first instance by the C.C.F. group, and never at any time assented to by the official opposition. So that I say the minister went very much farther than he undertook to go originally. The house divided and, in the light of all the circumstances, I think came to the only reasonable decision it could reach.
