These are some of the facts with regard to agreements which have been entered into. I may add that the contracts with Great Britain are for quantities which we estimated could be sent to Great Britain this year.
In so far as bacon and beef are concerned up to date we have greatly exceeded the quantities we had estimated at the beginning of the year. I should like to say, however, that it is probably too early to suggest that that production will keep up throughout the year. We estimate that the production of
hogs will be higher down to the middle of August than we had anticipated, and that there will probably be some drop off as compared with the production estimate from that period until the end of the year. But we do anticipate that we shall be able to fill this contract in quantity as it is now drawn during the present year.
So far as beef is concerned, deliveries there again have been higher in January and the early part of February than anyone anticipated. I should like to say in that connection that this was probably somewhat due to the fact that barley prices ran to quite a high level in January. There was a much heavier marketing of cattle during the month of January than anyone anticipated. The result of this was that cattle prices went down about one cent. Those prices have been coming back recently, and the run of cattle is not as high as it was in January. For that reason there is not as much grain being fed in Canada. I think the farmers anticipated that if prices ran along about where they were in the latter part of the year, and as we anticipated they would through that period, they would feed these cattle through until the end of April, as was their practice. But this year when prices went up to over $1.30 a bushel for barley in January, there were heavy shipments of cattle to market. Those heavy shipments placed more beef in the hands of the meat board to be shipped to Britain than was anticipated, but it is expected that, as we come toward spring when those cattle would have been normally delivered, the deliveries will be down as compared with previous estimates. The one may just about balance against the other. In other words, our deliveries down to about the end of April may not be greatly in excess of what was anticipated at the beginning of the year.
In stating that I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that that has something to do with the figures given today by the hon. member for Calgary West with regard to the increase in grain holdings in Canada at the present time. That grain is not now being fed to cattle that have already been slaughtered. There are results from that which I do not w-ish to discuss on this particular bill at this particular time. No doubt there will be a time during the session when we can discuss that matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side have no intention of delaying the discussion on this measure at this stage, but I wish to take a few minutes to state our position. I might say that the hon. member for Kamloops will be leaving and will not be able to contribute to the debate at a later stage; therefore he intends to take some part in the discussion tonight.
As the minister has stated, he is asking for the continuation for another year of the Agricultural Products Act. This act was passed in March of last year and was to be effective for one year or until the end of December if we met again in 1947, as we did. It was extended again in December, 1947, to be in effect until the end of March of this year, and now the minister is asking leave to introduce a bill to provide for its extension for another year.
It will be remembered that the original act gave the minister the power to take the farmers' crops and sell them at prices to be fixed in contracts with Great Britain. Some prices were already fixed, but others were to be fixed by the government. Under this amendment the minister is seeking the power to continue to make such agreements. As he says, this bill will continue the powers which he considers necessary to carry out the present agreements.
Some days ago we asked the minister to table the agreements. Later he gave some of us copies, but I do not believe the agreements were tabled because, as he said, they were not signed. I suggest that the minister indicate,

before we pass this stage, why agreements which were made in December are not signed by March, three months later?
Our general position on this measure is well known. We are opposed to it in principle. We are opposed1 to it because it is a complete negation of the form of marketing act which we favour and which the organized producers from one end of this country to the other are seeking. We favour an act based on the principle of provincially sponsored marketing boards operated by the organized farmers themselves.
The minister indicates and, of course, we all know that it is necessary to pass whatever legislation we are going to have within the next few days. Our opposition to this bill is one thing. It is well known. We do not propose to try to kill the bill by a long debate. We are, therefore, disposed not to delay it any longer at this time if I may speak for those associated with me, except for one address by the hon. member for Kamloops.
As I said, we favour marketing legislation of the nature I have outlined. We favour legislation which gives the producers themselves more say in the fixing of the prices of their products than is allowed them under this kind of legislation. We are opposed to the type of legislation which puts all price fixing powers in the hands of the government. We favour legislation of the nature of the Natural Products Marketing Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words. We supported the extension of this act the last time and we intend to support its extension at this time. However we are doubtful whether this is the proper method to adopt, to extend the act from one year to another. We doubt whether that will fulfil the purpose of the act, which is to carry out the contracts we have and to encourage further contracts with Great Britain in connection with basic agricultural products.
It seems to this group that if this act were permanent, if we did not have to renew it from year to year, it would give much more permanency to our contracts with Great Britain and increase our ability to make future contracts with that country. We would much prefer to see a permanent Agricultural Products Act in Canada which would give permanency to longterm contracts and provide for the orderly marketing of our agricultural products.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has outlined our position with respect to this measure, so that I shall confine my remarks to as short a space as possible. With other members of this party I am opposed to this

Agricultural Products Act
bill, to its principle and to every stage of its proceedings, because, unlike the hon. member -who has just taken his seat, I feel that the longer the Agricultural Products Act remains on the statute books in its present form, the more confused becomes the situation with respect to the marketing of agricultural products in Canada, and particularly the more difficult it becomes to get the type of marketing legislation that we wish to have, and which the farmers themselves wish to have, *namely, enabling legislation giving control over the marketing of their produce to producer boards.
Since our position is so well known, and since we have opposed this measure on each occasion it has been before the house-it has been before the house twice, once in its original form and once in the form of a temporary extension; we opposed it on both these occasions-it is not necessary to go in detail into the reasons why we are opposed to it. My remarks can be kept to a very brief compass.
I want to say at the outset, in outlining the reasons why we are opposed to it, that the first is the unwarranted assumption that the necessity of this particular legislation is based on a continuing emergency. We have slipped into the habit, it seems, of accepting government statements that there is a continuing emergency, while no longer requiring them to prove that as a fact. I feel, in passing, that it might be more realistic for the government to say that it is necessary in view of some impending emergency, and for them to direct their attention to the future, instead of making this unwarranted assumption that there is an emergency continuing from the past. If they did that there might be a basis in logic and reason for calling this emergency legislation. But since it is based on the so-called continuing emergency, I find no reason to agree with that view.
Second, the administration of the particular marketing policy of the government under this act has been such as to inflict serious losses on the farmers, and for that reason as well I am opposed to its continuation. The practice has been to force the farmers to carry the burden of national policy as represented in the contracts with the United Kingdom, under which Canada provides food at low prices to the people of that country. The result has been that the farmers alone have suffered the loss, instead of that loss being spread over the whole economy of Canada; while at the same time the effect of these contracts and the embargoes on exports to the United States, all tied up in this policy,
has been to freeze prices in Canada and to impose further losses on our agricultural producers.
The third reason why I cannot support the continuation of this act is that there is in it no proper provision to give a voice to the producers in the regulation of their own affairs. That can be seen by a study of the bill in general; but, without reading it, I refer particularly to section S, a brief study of which proves conclusively that the governor in council, the Minister of Agriculture, is the one who determines every aspect of prices, amounts produced, amounts sold, every aspect of our production and marketing, taking control away altogether from the farmers who do the work, grow the produce, and who are anxious to have legislation enabling them to regulate their own marketing.
What we need, what we demand, is a marketing act giving an opportunity to the producers to control their own production and their own sales, giving recognition to producer boards which are already established, and encouraging the establishment of other producer boards. This has been the cornerstone of the Progressive Conservative platform with regard to agricultural matters ever since this party has existed, and it has had a tremendous impetus, of course, since the leadership was taken over by the present leader of the opposition. This is a policy which reflects the view of organized agriculture; but in this particular case it is fair to say that, although we are frequently accused of being reactionary and behind the times, yet in this case-and it is not confined to this case-the policy of this party has preceded the expressed view of agricultural producers, of organized agriculture in this country, because in 1935 this party actually introduced such legislation, which, while perhaps not perfect in all its terms, did contain the principle which we have continued to advocate.
I should like to indicate briefly why, although we do not find in this legislation the kind of marketing proposals we advocate, we go farther and oppose the present act and ask that it be discontinued. We wish it eliminated so that a producers' marketing act may be substituted in its place. Last year, when the bill was first introduced the then hon. member for Yale outlined the position which we took with respect to this matter. In order to abbreviate my remarks, I think I cannot do better than quote two or three passages of what he had to say at that time. I am reading from Hansard of March 14, 1947, at page 1371:
We are not in accord with the principle involved in this bill. We do not consider it right
Agricultural Products Act

that the farmer who produces the product should have no say in its disposition or in the price he shall receive for it, and in that regard we are on all fours with the representations made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture a fortnight ago today.
He was referring to a meeting which had been held in Ottawa in March, 1947. He continued, further down the page:
The main reason why I am so strongly in favour of recognition of the boards at present in existence under the provincial marketing acts is that they are producer boards. The basis of those nine acts is just this, that in any stipulated area, if there be a majority of producers of certain commodities who desire to form themselves into a board, they may receive permission to do so. They elect their board, and that board carries out the control and the regulating of the marketing of the crops in an orderly fashion for the benefit of the producer, the benefit of the consumer and the benefit of trade, and it is only reasonable to my mind in a matter of this kind that the government should recognize the fact that such boards are in existence and that they are efficient.
The then hon. member for Yale accordingly moved on behalf of the official opposition an amendment to the bill, embodying our attitude with respect to marketing legislation. The amendment read as follows:
That the said bill be not now read the second time, but that it be resolved that an Agricultural Products Act should be based on the principle that producer boards, set up under provincial marketing acts, where such boards exist or as they may from time to time come into existence, be used for the purposes of such Agricultural Products Act, instead of commodity boards established by the minister under section four of the said bill.
This particular type of marketing legislation which was desired and which was contemplated in the amendment, which we desire to see in place of this act, affects most particularly a commodity grown in the province of British Columbia. I refer, of course, to apples. The uncertainty with respect to the future of the marketing of apples arises particularly through the loss of the British preference and through the lowering of tariffs against United States apples under the Geneva trade agreements. I have had consultations with representatives of apple growers, and they tell me that they are particularly concerned with regard to the marketing of their crop in the coming year. They have virtually no hope of getting into the British market; they are uncertain as to the competition which may come from the United States, and they are afraid that chaotic conditions of marketing in Canada may follow from the lack of overseas markets and the lack of effective powers in their own boards adequately to regulate marketing in Canada.

That is why they feel particularly that the time has now come that we should no longer delay the enactment of enabling legislation to give producer boards power to control and to regulate their own marketing within this country.
On this point I wish to make a brief reference to the loss of the British market and to emphasize why it is important that we in Canada should have marketing legislation of the type to which I refer. Officials who appeared before the senate committee to discuss the Geneva agreement and elimination of the British preference on apples have said that the reason why Canadian negotiators were willing to give up that preference was that the British market was very much less attractive now than it used to be. Their statement can be found in volume 2 of the proceedings of the standing committee of the senate on Canadian trade relations. If that were the case, and if the British market were actually less attractive than it was, then there might be good reason why we in Canada should look elsewhere for a market for apples.
I got in touch with the British food commission to check up on figures as to United Kingdom apple production, and I find that the figures they have do not substantiate the statement that the British apple market is less attractive to Canadian producers than it was before. It is true that, owing to the shortage of dollars, the British are not at the moment buying apples, but the officials referred to above went further and said that Great Britain has tremendously increased domestic production of apples, so that in the long range view the United Kingdom market is not as attractive to Canadian producers.
The figures given by the British food mission on British apple production do not bear out this contention. The number of apple-producing trees in Great Britain and Northern Ireland-I obtained the figures for the years before the war and after the war-is in each year approximately the same. Before the war they had 14,506,000 producing trees in 1938-39, and 15,245,000 in 1939-40; after the war in 1946-47, they had 14,799,000. Before the war, in 1938-39, the total consumption in the United Kingdom was 444,200 tons; after the war it was 451,300 tons. Domestic production for the years before and the first year

So that there is no increase in domestic production, nor is there an increase in the plantings of domestic trees, and therefore the figures do not bear out the statement made that the United Kingdom apple market is a less attractive market in the long run for Canadian producers.
That being the case, it is, I think, most regrettable that the Canadian apple producer has been faced with this reduction in the United Kingdom preference on apples, and of course it has confronted him with uncertainty as to the marketing of his crop in the future. Moreover, as I have said, it drives home the fact and makes more important than ever the necessity of introducing in Canada marketing legislation which will give the producer the responsibility and the opportunity of regulating the marketing of his own produce in an orderly fashion.
Last year, when the matter was being discussed, the minister indicated-I think it is fair to say he so indicated-general agreement with the principles put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on behalf of organized agriculture, but he said the time was not yet ripe to introduce the type of marketing legislation for which they were asking.
Here we are asked to renew the same act for another year, and no amendments have been made; there has been no progress toward the introduction of producer marketing legislation.
In closing, I wish to ask a number of questions and I hope the minister can give some answers to them before the resolution passes the committee. First, when may we expect to have the type of marketing legislation which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have been pressing for, which they pressed for last year, and which I have been discussing tonight? Second, what commodity boards have actually been established under the Agricultural Products Act as it exists at present, and with what provision for adequate producer representation? These are the words incorporated in the act, and I would be interested to know what producer representation has been provided for on the government commodity boards.
Another question is this. Would the minister give details of payments into and out of the agricultural products account since its creation under this act?
Finally, could he give the committee a rough estimate of the proportion of the total Canadian production which is going to Great Britain under the continuing contracts in connection with beef, eggs, cheese and bacon in
particular. Could the minister give an estimate of the proportion of total Canadian production represented in the supplies we have agreed to send over under these contracts?

speechtext: We support the idea of a commodity board because we believe in longterm international agreements. If you are to have such agreements you must have commodity boards, and we believe that such agreements are essential to Canadian agricultural production at a high level. But there is a question I would ask the minister. I believe the various farm organizations have asked the government to continue the Agricultural Prices Support Act as a permanent measure. Since that measure really underwrites the provisions of this measure, is it the intention of the government to make it a permanent measure? I understand that it is merely a transitional one at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1949
speechtext:
I have a few words to say on the measure. I shall be brief because I do not wish to delay the passage of it. First, I think it is generally recognized that agriculture is so interdependent on other parts of our economy that the general welfare of all Canadians has a distinct effect upon the wellbeing of this industry. In the last five or six years, as a result of the war economy, Canadians had reasonably full employment and good incomes. As a result of this condition, the consumption of agricultural products in Canada was the highest in history. More milk, butter, cheese, eggs and meat were consumed than ever before.
Agricultural Products Act

Second, the prosperity of agriculture in this country is also dependent on international good will. This is very true, since a good deal of Canadian agricultural produce enters world trade. Throughout the world today there is great need of agricultural products. The farmer could capitalize on that need by demands of excessive prices for his produce, but he prefers stabilized prices which are fair to farmer and consumer alike. He favours organized and orderly production and marketing in order that the production of farm products may be maintained to meet the world's needs.
Without that production the world will face malnutrition and, in some cases, virtual starvation. The production problem is closely related to the problem of distribution. In order to assist in the distribution of agricultural products, international commodity agreements are essential, especially in so far as the staple products are concerned, since these are always in demand on the international market. These staples include such commodities as wheat, bacon, cheese, beef, eggs and several others. I understand that this resolution has to do with the marketing of those agricultural products other than wheat.
The resolution before the house provides for the extension of the Agricultural Products Act until March 31, 1949. I have been informed that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in its presentation to the federal government at as recent a date as February 26, advocated floor prices for agricultural products and establishment of the Agricultural Prices Support Act as permanent legislation, with development, of course, of a fair statistical index which would indicate when support for agricultural prices is needed. I commend that program at this time to the government, I should like to suggest to the government that the Agricultural Products Act be retained until such time as federal marketing legislation is enacted. I feel that such legislation would be most acceptable to the farmer of Canada, especially if the farmer has some voice in the board that is set up under such legislation. The farmer would then know that his product will not be subject to the price fluctuations which, in the past, have been his unfortunate experience. The farmer is too often faced with insecurity, which is the natural result of speculative marketing of any kind. Most farmers have faced economic dilemmas because of the failure of governments to solve the marketing problem which often confronts the selling of agricultural produce. Mr. Henry Morgenthau, Junior, secretary of the United States treasury

under the Roosevelt administration, puts it aptly in the following words:
Of all the economic dilemmas which periodically confront us, the farmer's dilemma is one of the most terrible and, at the same time, one of the toughest to solve. When the farmer does not grow enough to satisfy the demand, prices rise, he makes a good living-and millions of people do not have enough to eat. When he raises too much, the bottom falls out of the market, he cannot keep up the payments on his mortgage, and his crops wither in the fields. The problem of the agricultural surplus is a tragic irony in the very centre of our economic system.
The extension of the Agricultural Products Act will help to solve this all too frequent economic dilemma; at least it will do that temporarily. I feel that much can yet be done to improve the lot of our producers. The government should now be considering federal marketing legislation to replace the act now before this house when it is discontinued one year from this date.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 1949

I rise to express my support of this measure. I shall not take up the time of the committee for long because I think unnecessary repetition is frightfully boring. In view of the representations of the agricultural organizations in this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, I think the time has come for this government to introduce federal marketing legislation. Experience justifies that act. We have the experience with provincial boards. Limited as they are through federal legislation, they have brought a measure of improvement to the agricultural producer. We have the experience through the War Measures Act in which the activities of various provincial boards were co-ordinated. I will say that the War Measures Act would not have functioned so efficiently had it not been for the provincial boards operating in various sections of the country.
We in Canada are falling sadly behind other countries with respect to agricultural marketing legislation. We have only to read the history of marketing boards and their development in Great Britain to realize that milk boards, potato boards, bacon boards and so on, are performing a necessary function. Those boards have been developed because of the necessity for them. Those boards were not introduced in the first instance, when they were originated in 1931, by a socialist government but by a Conservative government of Great Britain. I hope that this is the last time the minister will introduce a measure of this type into this house.
Before concluding, I wish to say that as far as I could hear I understood that the Progressive Conservative party oppose this

Agricultural Products Act
type of legislation. If they do, I would suggest that if their campaigners in the coming by-election in Yale tell the fruit growers of that constituency that such is their position, their vote will drop considerably.

The answer of the minister points up the fact that the government has no permanent policy in regard to an agricultural products marketing act. The stand of this group is clear. We want a permanent policy for the marketing of all agricultural products along the line of that provided for wheat, and oats and barley, if that ever goes through. On March 14 of last year, both the hon. member for Humboldt and the hon. member for Melfort moved the same amendment at different stages, and both were ruled out of order. Those amendments clearly state the position of the C.C.F. party. They read:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of
Agricultural Products Act

this house the government should give consideration to the redrafting of this bill to make provision for:
(a)	A dominion marketing board to have control over the orderly marketing of any farm product in interprovincial trade within Canada and in export trade;
(b)	Authority to confer on any existing local marketing board or agency established under law of a province, power to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovincial trade and export trade;
(c)	The establishment where any provincial local marketing board or agency does not exist, of local marketing boards to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovincial trade and export trade, providing the establishment of such a board is favoured by a majority of the producers in the area concerned, the membership of such a board to consist of producers of the regulated product in the area to which this scheme relates.
While members of this group have advocated permanent, adequate legislation, nevertheless we are willing to have this measure pass, though it be quite inadequate, because certainly it is better to have this measure for one year than to have no measure at all. I thought the hon. member for Middlesex West gave the Minister of Agriculture some good1 advice last year, and I hope he is still giving the same advice now that he has become his parliamentary assistant. On March 17, at page 1441 of Hansard, the hon. member for Middlesex West said:
I as a farmer, and representing farmers, am here tonight from western Ontario in this great old province of ours, to support this Bill No. 25. I feel that the minister is too modest in bringing down this legislation and making it operative for only one year. I think it should extend for two or three years instead of one.
I hope the hon. gentleman still thinks so; I hope he is still giving that advice to the minister, and I hope the minister will listen to him and bring in a proper agricultural products marketing act. It seems to me that one of the reasons we do not have proper production in the agricultural products with which we are dealing this evening is that the government has not gone to the farmers and told them it would implement adequate legislation to guarantee the farmers decent prices year in and year out. No one knows when the government may decide that the transitional period is at an end; therefore no one can tell, the farmers cannot tell, how long this legislation will remain in effect.
I am glad the minister has signed new contracts with Britain for this year, but I think we should be clear as to what those contracts amount to as compared with the contracts of

This year the minister has signed a contract providing for a minimum of 195,000,000 pounds of bacon, or just a little more than half the 1947 contract. The cheese contract for 1947 was for 125,000,000 pounds. The contract for this year is for only

I should like to make some observations which, to my mind, will help not only the farmer in this country in his production but will be of general benefit to the whole industry, particularly in connection with the export of bacon to the United Kingdom. As the minister well knows, during the last, two or three decades there has been a movement, probably led by Denmark, to reduce the weights of Wiltshire sides that are finding a market in the United Kingdom. The observation which I wish to make, speaking from experience-I think this will be borne out by hon. members-is this. The last ten pounds put on the hog before it is slaughtered are the easiest and cheapest ten pounds to put on. In view of that well-known fact the farmer makes his profit there. On the last ten pounds he makes a substantial profit. Has our policy been to encourage the British market to take a product a little heavier in weight, or are we still being led into a market which demands an even lighter weight or more lean and not so much fat? That has been the trend during the last thirty years. Has it started to turn the other way? If it has it should be encouraged to keep on in that way. If that were done the Canadian producer would find himself in a much more profitable position. It would increase our poundage for export with the same number of head of livestock; and as far as dietetics are concerned, in the judgment of many people who have studied this, it would be better for the people who are consuming the product if we reverse the trend a little. Has the minister's department made any study of that, and is he in a position to say that we are now down to the lightest possible weight, or are we able to increase the rate by four, five or six pounds? Even four, five or six pounds would be greatly to the benefit of the farmers of Canada; it would also benefit the consumers. What is the policy of the department in that regard?

LAURENT: Monday we shall take up, first of all, the resolution on the excise taxes, and when it is disposed of we shall proceed with the second reading and the committee stage of the bill which just received first reading. If any time remains after these are disposed of, the Minister of Veterans Affairs will go on with his resolution for leave to introduce a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
